solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Heading off to give credit to journalist

indicators.note: the head, or opening letter, of the credit word is cut away

parts.note: to ascribe something to someone is to credit them with it

explanation.surface: A news editor sends someone off to credit a reporter.
explanation.definitionFit: A scribe is a writer, and in journalese a reporter is often called one.

clue.text: Leave, determined to go on Scottish river

parts.note: set, as in set on something, means determined
the Forth is the river flowing into the Firth of Forth at Edinburgh

explanation.surface: Someone sets off, resolved to travel along a river in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means to start out on a journey, to depart.

clue.text: Prize dog not right after run out

indicators.note: the trimmed dog follows the run-out letters

parts.note: RO is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for run out

indicators.note: not means without the abbreviation for right

parts.note: a setter is a gun dog

explanation.surface: A prize-winning dog is disqualified after escaping.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket scorecards record a batsman dismissed 'run out' as RO.
explanation.definitionFit: A ribbon rosette is awarded as a prize at shows, including dog shows.

clue.text: Outspoken, expert about lake

indicators.note: about means the expert goes round the lake

parts.note: a buff is an enthusiast or expert

explanation.surface: A blunt specialist talks about a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Bluff describes a frank, hearty, direct manner, a synonym for plain-speaking.

clue.text: To that extent, illegally copy what Higgins taught Doolittle to do?

definitions.text: what Higgins taught Doolittle to do?

parts.note: as, as in 'as far as that', means to that degree
to pirate is to copy without permission

explanation.surface: A question about piracy linked to the teacher and flower girl of Pygmalion.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shaw's Pygmalion (My Fair Lady), Professor Higgins teaches Cockney Eliza Doolittle to sound her dropped H's.
explanation.definitionFit: To pronounce an initial h with breath is the phonetic sense, the skill Eliza lacked.

clue.text: Lone battle to secure plant

parts.note: solo means alone, lone
Mons was a First World War battle in Belgium
to seal is to secure or close up

explanation.surface: A single combatant fights to capture a factory.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodland perennial with arching stems and hanging white flowers, named for the biblical king.

clue.text: Among other things changed at airline

indicators.note: the letters of at airline are changed into a new order

explanation.surface: Several things changed at an airline.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase is used in English meaning 'including, besides others'.

clue.text: A sin involving a king's greed

indicators.note: the sin wraps round the a-and-king

parts.note: a vice is a sin
R is Rex, king

explanation.surface: A sin committed by a monarch is greed.
explanation.walkthrough: A comes first; VICE then holds A + R.
explanation.definitionFit: Avarice is the deadly sin of greed for wealth, an exact synonym.

clue.text: Very moving verse, start of "Ozymandias"

indicators.note: moving sets the letters of verse in motion, into a new order
the first letter of the poem's title is taken

explanation.surface: A very moving verse begins Shelley's poem Ozymandias.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' looks like 'touching' but is the anagram signal; 'start of' takes only the poem's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The colloquial intensifier, as in 'so kind', is a casual way of saying extremely.

clue.text: Concern shown after conclusion of government paper

indicators.note: the concern comes after the letter from government
the final letter of the word government is taken

parts.note: an issue is a matter of concern

explanation.surface: Worry is expressed after a government white paper ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Tissue paper is thin soft paper, so the word alone can name that kind of sheet.

clue.text: Knives and forks etc for an American's apartment are needed by wife

definitions.text: Knives and forks etc for an American

parts.note: a flat is the British word for an apartment

explanation.surface: An American's new apartment needs cutlery, and the wife insists on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for an American' belongs to the definition: the word is US usage for cutlery.
explanation.definitionFit: In American English, eating utensils collectively are called by this name.

clue.text: Welcome payments in precious metal? He will in different ones

parts.note: gold is a precious metal

indicators.note: the contracted pronoun-and-verb goes into the reordered word
different shows the letters of ones are rearranged

parts.note: he will contracts to he'll

explanation.surface: A puzzling question about precious metal and someone being among a different set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'different' is the anagram signal; 'in' puts the contraction inside. The question mark flags gold as figurative money.
explanation.definitionFit: These are lump sums paid to attract a new employee, the counterpart of golden handshakes.

clue.text: Below par, not in usual shape?

definitions.meaning: a playful literal reading: having left its regular figure or mould

explanation.surface: A sportsman is playing poorly and looks unfit.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means playing poorly; read literally it is being outside one's normal shape.

clue.text: Actor Claude, as painter in beginning of Séraphine

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, a painter

indicators.note: the opening letter of the name Séraphine is used

explanation.surface: An actor named Claude is cast as a painter in the opening of the film Séraphine.
explanation.definitionFit: Claude Rains was the English actor of Casablanca and The Invisible Man.

clue.text: Shetland leader lost in strait

indicators.note: lost suggests the letters have gone astray and are scrambled

explanation.surface: The leader of the Shetland Islands has gone missing in a narrow channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost' rearranges the fourteen letters of SHETLAND LEADER.
explanation.definitionFit: This narrow channel in Turkey links the Aegean with the Sea of Marmara.

clue.text: Completely over-the-top about pieces in plot

parts.note: all means completely, as in all alone

indicators.note: the exaggerated abbreviation goes round the pieces

parts.note: OTT is short for over the top
men are pieces in chess or draughts

explanation.surface: A story's plot becomes wholly exaggerated in places.
explanation.walkthrough: An allotment is a rented garden plot, common in Britain for growing vegetables.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot of land rented out for growing vegetables, so plot is a synonym.

clue.text: Left bishop inside, yet to lose

indicators.note: the bishop goes inside the leftover food

parts.note: uneaten food is left on the plate
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A chess team with its bishop kept back has not been beaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' is not the political or directional sense but leftover, as of food.
explanation.definitionFit: A team still undefeated has not yet lost a game, so the phrase is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Satisfying stop in place that sells juice

parts.note: a filling meal is satisfying
a station is a stop on a railway line

explanation.surface: A hearty stop at a place that sells fruit drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'juice' looks like fruit juice but is slang for fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: Juice is slang for petrol, and this is the roadside outlet that sells fuel.

clue.text: Scamp learning to beg

parts.note: an imp is a scamp, a rascal
lore is traditional knowledge or learning

explanation.surface: A rascal who is studying is pleading.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean to plead earnestly, a direct synonym; the infinitive matches the clue's 'to beg'.

clue.text: Up against it travelling to Spain

indicators.note: travelling puts the letters of to Spain on the move into a new order

explanation.surface: A traveller to Spain finds themselves in difficulties.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means in a difficult situation, facing trouble.

clue.text: Leave region after editor turned up

indicators.note: the region comes after the reversed editor
in a down clue turned up means read from bottom to top

parts.note: a part is a region, as in these parts

explanation.surface: Someone leaves an area after the newspaper editor arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned up' looks like 'arrived' but reverses ED into DE in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To depart is to go away, a straight synonym for leave as a verb.

clue.text: Cassette sent over intercepted by unknown emigrant

indicators.note: the reversed tape is broken into by the unknown
sent over means turned back to front

parts.note: a cassette is a tape
X is the algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A cassette mailed abroad is seized by a mysterious person who left the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent over' turns TAPE into EPAT, and X goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for expatriate, someone living outside their native country, as an emigrant does.

clue.text: Develop complex

definitions.meaning: as a verb, to expand on or add detail to
as an adjective, intricate and detailed

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to work out in more detail; as an adjective it means intricate.

clue.text: Old fine suspended

parts.note: nice means fine, pleasant

explanation.definitionFit: A plan put on ice is deferred, held in abeyance, so the idiom matches suspended.

clue.text: Not quite done during a dance, most importantly

indicators.note: the shortened word sits inside the a-plus-dance

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance

indicators.note: the word is left one letter short of complete

parts.note: over means finished, done

explanation.surface: An unfinished routine during a dance is the main thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not quite' drops the last letter of the word for done; 'during' places that inside a ball.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for 'chiefly' or 'more than anything else'.

clue.text: Allowed to adopt mischievous child, one not easily got rid of!

definitions.text: one not easily got rid of!

indicators.note: adopting takes the child into the family, so it goes inside

parts.note: let means allowed
an imp is a naughty child

explanation.surface: A couple are permitted to adopt a naughty child who then proves hard to shift.
explanation.definitionFit: A clinging hanger-on is called by the name of the shellfish that clamps to rocks.

clue.text: Paper in stand I look at briefly

parts.note: to stand someone a drink is to treat them

indicators.note: briefly means the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: to see is to look at

explanation.surface: Someone glances at a document on a stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stand' is not furniture but buying someone a drink, a treat; 'briefly' cuts the last letter from the looking verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper can be a scholarly essay, and a formal written study is a synonym.

clue.text: Church worker from Essex, tongue-tied

indicators.note: from shows the letters come out of the phrase Essex, tongue-tied

explanation.surface: A church employee from the county of Essex is lost for words.
explanation.walkthrough: Essex is a county east of London; the letters run across 'Essex, tongue'.
explanation.definitionFit: He looks after a church building and graveyard, traditionally ringing bells and digging graves.
